claims.label: Uncertainty relations
claims.summary: Heisenberg's uncertainty relations: the more precisely position is determined, the less precisely momentum can be known at that instant. He presented this as a limit set by the theory, not by instruments.
voice: The formalism itself sets the limit: the more precisely the position is fixed, the less precisely the momentum can be known at that instant, and conversely. This is not the clumsiness of our instruments. Any experiment capable of fixing the position must change the momentum in a way no refinement can compensate.
Position and momentum are not two quantities that we happen to measure badly together. The theory does not allow both to be sharp at once, and every experiment we can design respects that.
claims.reasoning: From the commutation relation pq − qp = h/2πi follows Δq·Δp of order h; every proposed measurement bears this out.
evidence: The Compton effect, which makes the recoil quantitative.
objections: Einstein: a limit on what can be known is not yet a limit on what is.
Bohr: the reasoning should rest on complementarity, not only on disturbance.
claims.later: Later work distinguished preparation uncertainty (Kennard 1927, Robertson 1929) from measurement disturbance; precise error–disturbance relations were derived and tested only in the 2000s–2010s.

claims.label: The path arises in observation
claims.summary: Heisenberg wrote that the classical 'path' comes into existence only when we observe it; between observations the question of where the electron really is has no definite physical content.
voice: I would put it sharply. The classical path of the electron is not something that is there and merely hidden from us. The path comes into being only when we observe it. Between observations, the question of where the electron really is has no definite physical content.
In the cloud chamber we see a row of droplets and call it a track. But each droplet is an observation, and what lies between them is not a path we failed to see.
claims.reasoning: A concept like position has meaning only through an experiment that defines it; the formalism assigns no path between such experiments.
objections: Einstein: this makes reality depend on observation.
Bohr: better to speak of the arrangement than of the observer.

claims.label: Causality fails
claims.summary: Heisenberg argued that the causal law — if we know the present exactly, we can calculate the future — fails not in its conclusion but in its premise, since the present cannot in principle be known in all its details. He called speculation about a real, causal world behind the statistical one fruitless and senseless.
voice: The law of causality says: if we know the present exactly, we can calculate the future. It is not the conclusion that is false but the premise. We cannot, in principle, know the present in all its details. To imagine a 'real' world hidden behind the statistical one, in which causality still holds, seems to me fruitless and senseless.
Physics should describe the connections between observations. Beyond that, a causal world that no experiment can ever reach is a matter of taste, not of science.
claims.reasoning: The uncertainty relations make the premise of strict causality unsatisfiable; a principle whose premise can never be met is empty.
objections: Lorentz: must indeterminism really be raised to a principle?
Planck: causality is a presupposition of inquiry, not an empirical claim.

claims.label: Only observable quantities
claims.summary: Heisenberg's 1925 paper set out to found quantum mechanics exclusively on relations between quantities that are in principle observable, discarding unobservable electron orbits.
voice: When I began, I resolved to use only quantities that can in principle be observed — the frequencies and intensities of spectral lines — and to drop the electron orbits that nobody has ever seen. That decision is what made the new mechanics possible.
The old theory failed because it insisted on orbits it could never verify. Remove them and the mathematics finds its own form.
claims.reasoning: The failures of the old quantum theory came from unobservable kinematic pictures.
evidence: Matrix mechanics reproduces spectral regularities that orbital models could not.
objections: Einstein: it is the theory that decides what is observable.

claims.label: A closed theory
claims.summary: The Born–Heisenberg report concluded that quantum mechanics is a closed theory whose fundamental physical and mathematical assumptions are no longer susceptible of modification.
voice: Born and I said it plainly in our report: we regard quantum mechanics as a closed theory. Its physical and mathematical foundations are no longer open to modification. Further experience will extend its application; it will not overturn its core.
I do not say there is nothing left to do — radiation, relativity, the nucleus. I say the principles we have are not provisional.
claims.reasoning: The theory is internally consistent, agrees with all experiments, and its statistical character follows from the uncertainty relations rather than from ignorance.
claims.later: The non-relativistic formalism has indeed survived unchanged; relativistic quantum field theory extended it. Whether it is 'complete' in Einstein's sense remains an interpretive question.

claims.label: Pictures redefined
claims.summary: Heisenberg rejected Schrödinger's physical picture of ψ as a real charge cloud, and in 1927 redefined 'anschaulich' to mean that one can think through the experimental consequences qualitatively, not that classical pictures return.
voice: Schrödinger's mathematics is splendid, and I use it every day. But his physical picture — electrons as smeared-out clouds of charge — cannot give Planck's law or the single events we count with a Geiger counter. We understand a theory intuitively when we can think through its experimental consequences in every simple case. That is what I mean by anschaulich — not the return of the old pictures.
Privately I have said harsher things about Schrödinger's claims to visualisability than I would say here. The substance is the same: the picture does not survive contact with discrete events.
claims.reasoning: Wave pictures fail for many-particle systems and for discrete processes; understanding is qualitative mastery of consequences.

claims.label: The observer makes the choice
claims.summary: In the general discussion Heisenberg disagreed with Dirac's statement that nature makes a choice in measurement, saying rather that the observer makes it, since only at the moment of observation does the 'choice' become a physical reality.
voice: I do not agree with Dirac that nature makes the choice. Even long afterwards one may, in principle, arrange things so that the alternatives interfere. I should rather say that the observer makes the choice, because only at the moment the observation is made has the 'choice' become a physical reality.
claims.reasoning: As long as interference between alternatives remains possible in principle, no choice has been made; it is the act of observation that settles it.
claims.exchangeNote: General discussion of the fifth Solvay council, as recorded in the proceedings.
claims.later: The question of when a 'choice' becomes irreversible was later addressed by decoherence theory.

claims.label: The gamma-ray microscope
claims.summary: Heisenberg's thought experiment: locating an electron precisely requires short-wavelength light, whose quantum gives the electron an unknowable Compton recoil.
voice: Consider a microscope that uses gamma rays to locate an electron. To see it sharply we need short wavelengths; but a short-wavelength quantum striking the electron gives it a Compton recoil we cannot fully know. Sharpen the position and you blur the momentum. It is Compton's effect that makes the argument quantitative.
claims.reasoning: Resolution and recoil trade off exactly as the uncertainty relation requires.
